answers.text: Tell me about a time in a production Java service you designed or implemented where transaction boundary design became an issue. Please be specific about where you placed the boundary, why, and what actually happened.
answers.answer: I work on the employer withholding reconciliation system for a state tax agency — the part that matches what employers report and pay in quarterly against what actually clears. For the first two of my four years there, the payment-posting endpoint recorded the payment and then, inside that same transaction, kicked off an audit-risk calculation for the employer, because someone figured it was simpler to keep them atomic. During the quarter-end filing window, when a huge share of our roughly 600,000 employers file within about three days of each other, that calculation could take a second or two under load, and it held the lock on the employer's account row the whole time. I split it out: the payment posts in its own fast transaction, and a separate worker picks up the audit-risk calculation from a queue afterward. The first version of that worker silently swallowed errors instead of retrying, so for about six hours after I shipped it, a batch of employers with a particular data format didn't get their risk score updated at all until I noticed the queue backlog and added real retry and alerting logic.
answers.says: Names a concrete transaction-boundary problem in a production Java service they were responsible for (e.g., lock contention on a long transaction, an external API call left inside a transaction, inconsistency from an isolation level), describes where they moved the boundary and the grounds for that decision (measurements, a real incident, data-consistency requirements), and covers the outcome or the fix for a failure, with numbers and time frames. Beyond just ‘we did it as a team,’ their own judgment and hands-on work are clear, and they can explain a design failure in their own words.

answers.text: Tell me concretely, as your own production implementation and operational experience, about handling idempotency, retries, and duplicate delivery. Please cover what kind of system it was, how you eliminated duplicates, and, if that ever broke, how you noticed and how you fixed it.
answers.answer: Employer withholding payments get an idempotency key made of employer ID, filing period, and the payment processor's own transaction reference, enforced with a unique index. It failed us once: during a scheduled maintenance window on the payment processor's side, our retry logic resent about 210 payments that had actually gone through but hadn't yet returned a confirmation before the window started, and for those, the transaction reference we'd stored was a temporary one that got replaced by a permanent reference afterward — so the unique constraint didn't catch the duplicates because the keys genuinely looked different. That was roughly $340,000 in overstated employer payments. Our nightly reconciliation against the processor's settlement file caught the mismatch the next morning. We reversed the duplicates with new corrective entries and changed the key to use the employer-submitted reference instead of the processor's temporary one, since that one doesn't change.
answers.says: Names the concrete mechanism they implemented and operated (idempotency-key design, store choice, duplicate-delivery detection, reconciliation mechanism), why they chose that design, and the process of noticing and recovering when an incident or duplication actually occurred, with numbers (scale, count, time taken) and time frames. If it was an experience of resolving a consistency mismatch, they can also describe the root-cause triage and the grounds for correcting it with a new journal entry or record rather than an overwrite.

answers.text: Tell me about an incident that occurred in a system you operated. Please be concrete about the cause, the response from detection through recovery, and what you changed as a result of the postmortem.
answers.answer: That duplicate-payment issue is the incident I'd point to. Detection was the next morning's reconciliation report, so from the actual duplicates going in to us noticing, it was overnight — longer than I'd want. Once I saw the mismatch, I pulled the payment logs and had the root cause, the temporary-versus-permanent reference issue, narrowed down within about 45 minutes. I looped in my lead and our finance liaison as soon as I had a number on how many employers were affected, before I'd written a single line of the fix. Getting the reversing entries posted and verified against the processor's file took about four hours total. Out of the postmortem, we moved reconciliation to run every couple hours instead of nightly, so a gap like that would surface same-day now instead of the next morning.
answers.says: Describes an incident in a system they operated, with a timeline and numbers (time from detection, time to recovery, number of affected cases). Explains, in their own words, what they looked at to triage the cause and the recovery decisions (including who they told and when), and can describe the postmortem's preventive measures and whether they actually worked afterward. If their own mistake caused it, they can describe, matter-of-factly, how they shared that without hiding it.

answers.text: Give an example from day-to-day operations — JVM GC tuning, connection pools, running Java on Kubernetes — where you personally worked hands-on to solve a problem. Tell me what you measured, what you changed, and what changed as a result.
answers.answer: During that same quarter-end window we'd get thread pool exhaustion on the API layer — not the DB connection pool, the actual request-handling thread pool, because a slow downstream call to our identity-verification service was tying up threads for the full length of the call. I put a timeout and a circuit breaker around that call so a slow dependency couldn't starve the whole thread pool, and separately increased the pool size after checking what the box could actually handle. Requests that used to queue for several seconds during peak filing hours came back under 200ms once both changes were in.
answers.says: Names a concrete operational problem in a Java service they operated (e.g., latency degradation from GC pauses, connection pool exhaustion, an OOM on Kubernetes), and describes the measurement tools used, the numbers obtained, the changes tried, the results (with figures), and, if the first fix missed, the failure and the retry. Can explain the triage process in their own words, with grounds for the decisions rather than a list of tool names.

answers.text: Have you ever, while responding to an urgent incident, felt tempted to skip review or the normal deployment procedure? Tell me what you actually did, and what you think would need to be in place to justify a decision to skip a step.
answers.answer: During that incident, I pushed the reference-key fix without waiting for our usual second reviewer, because the maintenance window issue could recur on the processor's side and I didn't want more duplicates landing while I found someone available at that hour. I said exactly that in our team channel before I deployed — what I was changing and that I was skipping the second review because of the circumstances — and then opened a proper PR the next day so it actually got reviewed. Outside of a situation like that, where real money is moving wrong in the meantime, I don't skip it. Being sure of a fix isn't the same thing as someone else having actually looked at it.
answers.says: Names a concrete experience of being forced to choose between the procedure and an emergency, and describes what they actually did. If they skipped it, they describe the steps — announcing it beforehand, recording it afterward, and following up with the normal procedure once recovered — together with the criteria for that skip decision. If they didn't skip it, they describe why (not shipping a change they can't verify, money is not a test environment) and an alternative way to move quickly and safely without cutting the procedure. Either way, their own judgment and its outcome come through as a concrete example.

answers.text: Tell me about your experience and thinking on migrating from Java to Rust. If you have production Rust experience, tell me its scope; if not, tell me how you think you could realistically learn the differences from Java — ownership, lifetimes, async runtimes. Also tell me your thinking on how to decide a service boundary.
answers.answer: I should just say it plainly — I haven't written Rust, in production or otherwise. I know the general shape of the pitch, ownership and borrow checking replacing a garbage collector to prevent certain classes of bugs at compile time, but that's about where my knowledge stops. I don't have a real learning plan mapped out yet either, if I'm being honest — it hasn't been something my work required, so I haven't pushed myself to sit down with it. I'd rather tell you that straight than dress it up with a timeline I haven't actually thought through.
answers.says: Can describe Rust terminology accurately (ownership, lifetimes, tokio, etc.), but gives no real example of code they wrote or ran themselves. On migration too, the answer stays at generalities like ‘Rust should be adopted because it's safe and fast,’ without describing how to decide a boundary or what to measure as their own judgment. The explanation of the difference from Java reads like a summary of an introductory book, and the learning plan is no more than ‘I'll study it,’ with no realism visible.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you shared a mistake or a delay early, and about your experience with on-call, handling inquiries, or mentoring juniors. For both, please be concrete about what you yourself did.
answers.answer: Smaller story, but it's mine: I once deployed a change to how we calculate late-filing penalties that had an off-by-one error in the day count, and I caught it myself about half an hour later when a penalty amount on my own test employer looked wrong. I flagged it in the team channel right away, before anyone else had noticed, and rolled it back the same afternoon. I've been on the on-call rotation for this system for about three years, one week in five, and quarter-end weeks are genuinely busy — I've had shifts with six or seven pages. I've also spent real time walking a newer engineer through how the reconciliation reports work, since that's usually the hardest part of this system to get comfortable with.
answers.says: Can describe a concrete example of sharing their own mistake or delay before it got worse — what, when, to whom, how it was communicated, and what happened as a result. Also names a real example of taking on on-call rotation, inquiry handling, or mentoring juniors as their own job (duration, frequency, approach), and can describe never having thought of it as ‘not my real job.’ Both are told as their own actions, including experience of sharing within a blameless culture.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you restored data consistency in a production Java service after an incident or a bug. What was broken, how did you pin down the scope, how did you fix it, and how did you confirm the fix worked?
answers.answer: A data issue came up when two employer records got merged incorrectly after a name-change filing — the merge logic kept one employer's withholding history but dropped about 60 payment records that belonged to the other employer in the pair, over roughly an 18-month lookback window. I scoped it by querying our audit log for merge events in that period and cross-referencing which payment records had an employer ID that no longer existed after the merge. I fixed it by inserting the missing records under the correct employer ID rather than trying to patch the merged record, then verified by recomputing each affected employer's total withholding and checking it against their own filed W-2 equivalents. My first pass only caught merges from one specific filing form; a second form type triggered the same bug and I found that only after re-running the audit query with broader criteria.
answers.says: Names a concrete inconsistency in a production service they were responsible for (e.g., double counting, a missing journal entry, a batch job that stopped partway), and describes how they scoped the impact (query, count, time period), how they fixed it (a correcting record rather than an overwrite, a backfill), and how they verified the fix afterward (reconciliation, recalculation), with numbers. Can also describe it if their first read of the problem was wrong.

answers.text: If you were to move part of the ledger write path to Rust, where would you start, where would you place the boundary with Java, and what would you measure before and after the migration to make that call? If you've cut out a language or service boundary before, please answer in light of that experience.
answers.answer: I don't have hands-on experience here, Rust or any other language migration, so this is more reasoning from first principles than something I've actually done. My instinct would be to pick the narrowest, most self-contained piece — something that doesn't need to share a database transaction with the rest of the system — and put real numbers around it before and after: latency, error rate, maybe memory if that's the concern. I'd also want a period where the new piece runs alongside the old one and gets compared before it actually takes over live traffic. But I want to be honest that I'm describing what seems sensible, not something I've watched work or fail firsthand.
answers.says: Can describe a general direction for migration, but it stays at generalities (‘measurement matters first,’ ‘migrate in stages’), without describing the concrete boundary location, the metrics to watch, or the decision criteria in their own words. Even when citing past experience carving out a boundary, they can't distinguish what they decided from ‘what the team did,’ and no numbers or failures come up.

answers.text: We don't do full rewrites. What kind of part do you think should not be moved to Rust? If you've ever held back the urge to rewrite something and kept it in Java or an existing language, tell me about that too.
answers.answer: I can't speak to Rust specifically since I haven't used it, but I have a real example of holding back a rewrite in Java. After that employer-merge bug, I wanted to redesign the whole merge system from scratch — it felt fragile in a few places I could see. The team pushed back that we didn't have time before the next filing season and that the actual bug was narrower than the whole system, so I scoped it down to fixing the specific merge-form gap instead of the full redesign. In general, my sense is you don't rewrite something because it feels fragile — you rewrite it once you've actually measured where it's failing and the cost of leaving it is clearly higher than the cost of the change.
answers.says: Describes the criteria for deciding not to move something in their own words, and names a concrete experience of actually holding back the urge to rewrite — what, why, how they measured it, and how they reached agreement with the team. The grounds for separating what to migrate from what not to are based on measurement and agreement.

fit.says: Considering what it would be like for this person to work here, they can be judged as someone who would act in line with all of our working principles (argue with evidence, then follow the decision; do not hide; money is not a test environment; operations and support are equal work; decide the boundary before you rewrite). Throughout the candidate's account of their experience, they consistently show a stance of sharing incidents and mistakes without hiding them, treating on-call, support, and mentoring juniors as their own job, never skipping review and deployment procedures even in an emergency, and carrying out migrations based on measurement and agreement while respecting the team's decisions.
